content.text:
For a **typical cold**, there’s no medicine that cures it—treatment is mainly to **relieve symptoms** while it runs its course. Most colds improve on their own in about **7–10 days**, though cough can last longer. Antibiotics **don’t help** a cold because colds are caused by viruses. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/treatment/index.html?utm_source=openai))

**Choose based on your symptoms:**

- **Fever, headache, body aches, sore throat:**  
  **Acetaminophen** or **ibuprofen** can help. Follow the label, and avoid doubling up—many “multi-symptom” cold products already contain acetaminophen. ([mayoclinic.org](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/common-cold/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20351611?sf237848573=1&utm_source=openai))

- **Stuffy nose/congestion:**  
  Try **saline spray/rinse**, steam/humidifier, and fluids. A decongestant may help some people, but avoid or ask a clinician first if you have **high blood pressure, heart disease, glaucoma, prostate/urination problems, are pregnant, or take certain medications**.

- **Cough:**  
  Warm fluids and **honey** may soothe cough—**do not give honey to children under 1 year**. Some adults use cough suppressants like **dextromethorphan**, but results vary.

- **Runny nose/sneezing:**  
  Some antihistamines can dry secretions but may cause **drowsiness**, dry mouth, or interact with other medicines.

**Children:** Be extra careful. The FDA says children **under 2** should not be given cough/cold products containing a decongestant or antihistamine because of serious risks; for older children, use caution and follow pediatric dosing directions. Also, don’t give **aspirin** to children or teenagers. ([fda.gov](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/safe-use-over-counter-otc-medicines-children/use-caution-when-giving-cough-and-cold-products-kids?utm_source=openai))

**Call a doctor/clinic urgently** if you have trouble breathing, chest pain, severe weakness, dehydration, confusion, symptoms that worsen after improving, fever lasting more than ~3 days, or symptoms lasting more than 10 days. Also consider **COVID/flu testing**, especially if you’re high-risk, because antivirals work best early. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/treatment/index.html?utm_source=openai))

If you tell me your **age**, main symptoms, any medical conditions, and medicines you already take, I can help you choose a safer OTC option.
